idiom_name: method taking a block, calling yield per element (each-style producer)
implementation_notes: The Ruby generator is a method that yields to the caller's block: production happens inside the method, the block runs once per element, and break or next in the block controls continuation - internal iteration with on-demand production and no state machine to hand-write. Return an Enumerator (variant) - via enum_for/to_enum or Enumerator.new - when callers need a first-class object to pass around, compose or pull from; the block form stays the idiomatic first choice for a single consuming loop.
code_sketch:
def fib(limit = nil)          # yields one element at a time
  a, b, n = 0, 1, 0
  while limit.nil? || n < limit
    yield a                   # consumer decides when to stop
    a, b = b, a + b
    n += 1
  end
end

fib { |x| break if x > 100; puts x }
pitfalls: A method that yields unconditionally raises LocalJumpError when called without a block; guard with block_given? (or return to_enum(:fib, limit)) so one method serves both push and pull consumers.
break inside the block unwinds through the producing method, so code after the yield loop does not run unless it is wrapped in ensure; file or lock cleanup belongs in ensure, not after the loop.
Blocks capture the caller's binding: returning a lambda or an Enumerator that closes over large locals keeps them alive, so long-lived enumerators can pin memory.

variants.name: Enumerator / Enumerator::Lazy (Fiber-backed pull generator)
variants.idiom_name: Enumerator.new { |y| ... } / enum_for(:each_x) with next, peek and .lazy
variants.implementation_notes: Enumerator turns any yielding method into a first-class external iterator: to_enum/enum_for wraps the method, Enumerator.new builds one from a block with a yielder, and next/peek pull elements one at a time (StopIteration marks the end, rewind restarts where possible). Enumerator::Lazy (Ruby 2.0) adds map/select/take chaining that stays lazy, which is how infinite sources are consumed safely. It is implemented with Fibers, so each Enumerator allocates a stack and every element pays a context switch - use it for composition, not for hot loops.
variants.code_sketch:
enum = Enumerator.new do |y|          # explicit generator
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }    # infinite source
end

enum.lazy.select(&:even?).first(3)    # => [0, 2, 4]; stops early
enum.next                             # => 0, then 1, 2 ...
pitfalls: External iteration runs the producer on a Fiber, so the stack trace stops at the Enumerator boundary and each element costs a context switch; hot loops should use the block form instead.

next raises StopIteration when exhausted and cannot be reset (rewind works only for rewindable enumerators); re-iterate the underlying method rather than reusing a spent enumerator, and remember that each call to an Enumerator.new block restarts the source.
